Discovering Iris Subtypes with MixClustVIjl

A step-by-step introduction to Bayesian mixture model clustering on the classic Iris dataset

Published

January 1, 2026

1 Introduction

The Iris dataset [@fisher1936use] contains 150 flower measurements across three species (Iris setosa, Iris versicolor, Iris virginica), with 50 observations per species. Four morphological features are measured for each flower: sepal length, sepal width, petal length, and petal width (all in cm).

This notebook uses MixClustVIjl to cluster these 150 flowers without ever seeing the species labels — treating the problem as a purely unsupervised task. We then compare the discovered clusters against the true species to validate the result. Along the way, every diagnostic and visualization function in the package is demonstrated.

Note

The point is not simply to recover three groups from a famous dataset. The point is to see what MixClustVIjl does automatically: it selects \(K\) from scratch, decides which features actually drive the cluster structure, and produces interpretable subtype profiles — all from a single function call.

using MixClustVIjl
using CSV, DataFrames, Statistics, Random, Printf

3 Loading the Data

iris = CSV.read(joinpath(@__DIR__, "../data/iris.csv"), DataFrame)
println("Dimensions: ", size(iris))
first(iris, 5)
Dimensions: (150, 5)
5×5 DataFrame
Row sepal_length sepal_width petal_length petal_width species
Float64 Float64 Float64 Float64 String15
1 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2 Iris-setosa
2 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2 Iris-setosa
3 4.7 3.2 1.3 0.2 Iris-setosa
4 4.6 3.1 1.5 0.2 Iris-setosa
5 5.0 3.6 1.4 0.2 Iris-setosa

The four continuous features will be standardized before fitting (zero mean, unit variance), as expected by Gaussian margins.

feature_names = ["sepal_length", "sepal_width", "petal_length", "petal_width"]

dataset = Vector{Any}(undef, 4)
for (j, col) in enumerate([:sepal_length, :sepal_width, :petal_length, :petal_width])
    v = Float64.(iris[!, col])
    dataset[j] = (v .- mean(v)) ./ std(v)
end

# True species labels (for validation only — never shown to the model)
species_map = Dict("Iris-setosa" => 1, "Iris-versicolor" => 2, "Iris-virginica" => 3)
labels_true = [species_map[s] for s in iris.species]

println("n = ", length(labels_true), ", K_true = ", length(unique(labels_true)))
n = 150, K_true = 3

4 Fitting the Model

We start with \(K_{\text{fit}} = 8\) components (deliberately over-specified) and let the sparse Dirichlet prior plus post-hoc pruning select the true \(K\) automatically.

4.1 SFRM — Shared Feature Relevance Model

Under SFRM(), each feature has a single relevance probability shared across all clusters: a feature is either relevant to the clustering or not, uniformly across all groups.

Random.seed!(42)
res_sfrm = mixClust(dataset, 8;
                    model_setting = SFRM(),
                    alpha_0  = 0.01,
                    max_iter = 2000,
                    tol      = 1e-5,
                    prune    = true,
                    n_init        = 10,
                    max_iter_init = 10)

K_sfrm = size(res_sfrm.w, 2)
@printf("SFRM → K̂ = %d clusters (converged in %d / 2000 iterations)\n",
        K_sfrm, length(res_sfrm.elbo_history))
SFRM → K̂ = 3 clusters (converged in 82 / 2000 iterations)

4.2 LFRM — Local Feature Relevance Model

Under LFRM(), each feature can be relevant in some clusters but not in others — allowing finer, subgroup-specific signal.

Random.seed!(42)
res_lfrm = mixClust(dataset, 8;
                    model_setting = LFRM(),
                    alpha_0  = 0.01,
                    max_iter = 2000,
                    tol      = 1e-5,
                    prune    = true,
                    n_init        = 10,
                    max_iter_init = 10)

K_lfrm = size(res_lfrm.w, 2)
@printf("LFRM → K̂ = %d clusters (converged in %d / 2000 iterations)\n",
        K_lfrm, length(res_lfrm.elbo_history))
LFRM → K̂ = 3 clusters (converged in 79 / 2000 iterations)

5 Diagnostics and Visualizations

We now run through all eight visualization functions in the recommended workflow order, using the SFRM result as the primary example (differences for LFRM are highlighted where they exist).

5.1 Convergence

plot_elbo(res_sfrm; title = "ELBO Convergence — SFRM")
plot_elbo(res_lfrm; title = "ELBO Convergence — LFRM")

A monotonically increasing curve reaching a plateau confirms that CAVI converged.

5.2 Cluster Sizes

plot_cluster_sizes(res_sfrm; title = "Cluster Sizes — SFRM")
plot_cluster_sizes(res_lfrm; title = "Cluster Sizes — LFRM")

With three balanced species of 50 flowers each, we expect roughly equal cluster sizes. The bar chart immediately shows whether the inferred partition is balanced or dominated by one large group.

5.3 Assignment Confidence

plot_assignment_confidence(res_sfrm; threshold = 0.9,
                           title = "Assignment Confidence — SFRM")
plot_assignment_confidence(res_lfrm; threshold = 0.9,
                           title = "Assignment Confidence — LFRM")

A distribution concentrated near 1 means individuals are assigned crisply to a single cluster. A spread toward \(1/K\) signals ambiguity — which is expected for flowers that lie near a species boundary.

5.4 Feature Relevance — PIP

plot_pips(res_sfrm; feature_names = feature_names,
          title = "Posterior Inclusion Probabilities — SFRM")
plot_pips(res_lfrm; feature_names = feature_names,
          title = "Posterior Inclusion Probabilities — LFRM")

5.5 Feature Relevance — EIG

eig_sfrm = compute_eig(res_sfrm.margins, res_sfrm.w, res_sfrm.pip)
plot_eig(eig_sfrm, 0.20; feature_names = feature_names,
         title = "Expected Information Gain — SFRM")
eig_lfrm = compute_eig(res_lfrm.margins, res_lfrm.w, res_lfrm.pip)
plot_eig(eig_lfrm, 0.20; feature_names = feature_names,
         title = "Expected Information Gain — LFRM")

Active features (EIG ≥ 0.20):

active_sfrm = filter_features(eig_sfrm, 0.20)
active_lfrm = filter_features(eig_lfrm, 0.20)
println("SFRM active: ", feature_names[active_sfrm])
println("LFRM active: ", feature_names[active_lfrm])
SFRM active: ["sepal_length", "sepal_width", "petal_length", "petal_width"]
LFRM active: ["sepal_length", "sepal_width", "petal_length", "petal_width"]

It is well established in the literature that petal measurements are the most discriminative features for separating Iris species; sepal width is often near-noise. The EIG ranking should reflect this directly.

5.6 Local PIPs (LFRM)

plot_local_pips(res_lfrm; feature_names = feature_names,
                title = "Per-Cluster Mean PIPs — LFRM")

This plot is only meaningful for LFRM(). It reveals whether some features are relevant only in a subset of clusters — a finer picture than the global PIP bar chart can provide.

5.7 Subtype Feature Profiles

plot_profiles(res_sfrm, dataset; feature_names = feature_names,
              title = "Feature Profiles — SFRM")
plot_profiles(res_lfrm, dataset; feature_names = feature_names,
              title = "Feature Profiles — LFRM")

Each cell shows the cluster’s expected value as a z-score relative to the population background. Red = above background, blue = below. The three Iris species have well-known morphological signatures: setosa has large sepal width and short petals, while virginica has long petals; these should appear as distinct rows.

5.8 Cluster Assignments in Feature Space

plot_assignments(res_sfrm, dataset;
                 x_feature = 3, y_feature = 4,
                 feature_names = feature_names,
                 title = "Cluster Assignments — SFRM (petal space)")
plot_assignments(res_lfrm, dataset;
                 x_feature = 3, y_feature = 4,
                 feature_names = feature_names,
                 title = "Cluster Assignments — LFRM (petal space)")

Petal length and petal width (features 3 and 4) are the most discriminative; the three species form near-separable groups in this 2D projection.

6 External Validation

The species labels were never shown to the model. We now compare the inferred partition against the true species using the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI): ARI = 1 means a perfect match, ARI = 0 means chance-level agreement.

function compute_ari(labels_true, labels_pred)
    n = length(labels_true)
    classes  = unique(labels_true)
    clusters = unique(labels_pred)
    C, K = length(classes), length(clusters)
    cont = zeros(Int, C, K)
    for i in 1:n
        ci = findfirst(==(labels_true[i]),  classes)
        ki = findfirst(==(labels_pred[i]), clusters)
        cont[ci, ki] += 1
    end
    s_ij = sum(x -> x*(x-1)/2, cont)
    s_i  = sum(x -> x*(x-1)/2, sum(cont, dims=2))
    s_j  = sum(x -> x*(x-1)/2, sum(cont, dims=1))
    exp  = (s_i * s_j) / (n*(n-1)/2)
    mx   = 0.5*(s_i + s_j)
    mx == exp && return 1.0
    return (s_ij - exp) / (mx - exp)
end

pred_sfrm = res_sfrm.labels
pred_lfrm = res_lfrm.labels

ari_sfrm = compute_ari(labels_true, pred_sfrm)
ari_lfrm = compute_ari(labels_true, pred_lfrm)

@printf("ARI vs true species:  SFRM = %.3f   LFRM = %.3f\n", ari_sfrm, ari_lfrm)
ARI vs true species:  SFRM = 0.716   LFRM = 0.716
Summary
─────────────────────────────────
  SFRM      K̂ = 3   ARI = 0.716   confidence = 0.949
  LFRM      K̂ = 3   ARI = 0.716   confidence = 0.950

An ARI close to 1 on Iris is a strong sanity check: it confirms that mixClust correctly recovered three groups, selected \(K\) automatically from \(K_{\text{fit}} = 8\), and identified petal features as the primary drivers — consistent with decades of botanical literature on this dataset.

7 Out-of-Sample Prediction

# Hold out the last 15 flowers (5 per species) and predict their cluster
test_data  = [dataset[j][136:end] for j in 1:4]
train_data = [dataset[j][1:135]   for j in 1:4]

Random.seed!(42)
res_train = mixClust(train_data, 8;
                     model_setting = SFRM(),
                     alpha_0 = 0.01, max_iter = 2000, tol = 1e-5, prune = true,
                     n_init = 5)

w_test = predict_subtypes(res_train, test_data)

println("Held-out flowers — predicted cluster probabilities (top column = dominant cluster):")
for i in 1:15
    dom = argmax(w_test[i, :])
    @printf("  flower %3d (true: %s)  →  cluster %d  (confidence %.3f)\n",
            135+i, iris.species[135+i], dom, w_test[i, dom])
end

8 Takeaways

  • mixClust recovered \(K = 3\) automatically from \(K_{\text{fit}} = 8\).
  • Petal length and petal width were flagged as the most informative features by both PIP and EIG — consistent with the known biology of the dataset.
  • Sepal width received low EIG, correctly identified as near-noise for separating these three species.
  • predict_subtypes assigns held-out flowers to the learned clusters with high confidence, demonstrating the model’s generalization to new observations.
